quote: No. The thing is the person said that, you guys have a Delta solar panel for me to take a look at. But I was saying I already have solar panel. All I needed was, like, batteries.
stewart_read: This is an orphaned-flow scenario (existing solar owner) combined with a battery-only ask — outside the standard new-install script. The rep does not run any of the orphaned_flow qualifying questions (owns vs. leases the existing system, which company installed it, is it working).
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive miss — rep simply didn't know the orphaned_flow questions applied here.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to run the three orphaned-system qualifiers (ownership type, installer, system working) even on a battery-only call — a leased/PPA system or a broken system are hard DQs Ion cannot service, and this could be wasting a closer's appointment slot.

quote: let me look at yeah. It says it's just for a battery. That's just a generic text that goes out.
stewart_read: The customer just handed the rep a clean anchor (battery-only need on an existing solar system) and the rep filed it as an administrative note rather than asking why she wants a battery now (power outages? new usage? distrust of grid?).
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic — the rep may be deliberately keeping the call short since it's purely a scheduling call and the closer will explore motivation. This is plausible given the call's brevity and pure-logistics shape.
coaching_implication: Even a 30-second 'what's got you looking at a battery now?' would give the closer a motivational anchor. Flag as a quick, low-cost addition rather than a hard failure.

quote: Would you be able to talk about that battery tomorrow?
stewart_read: This begins a five-round scheduling negotiation with no structural anchor (no stated call length, no 'is that fair' handshake) until the very end. The rep is proposing times without framing what the appointment actually covers.
coaching_implication: Even on a short battery-focused call, anchor the appointment length and purpose early ('it's about a 30-minute call to look at battery backup options') so the customer is scheduling with clear expectations, not just picking a time blind.

quote: I'll shoot you a text so you have it in writing. Okay?
stewart_read: The rep does promise a text follow-up, which is good procedure, but the button-up otherwise skips the one-hour block statement, the no-driving/computer instruction, and any recap of what the appointment will cover.
coaching_implication: Add the missing button-up elements (call length expectation, no-driving/at-computer ask) even on a short scheduling-only call — these are predictive of show rate per the script.

quote: Yeah. Looks like we were supposed to meet with you about a month ago. We just weren't able to.
stewart_read: The rep opens by referencing internal scheduling history rather than establishing who he is, what company, and why he's calling — no company name beyond 'This is Carter' at the very top, no state, no legitimacy framing.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic — the customer initiated by saying 'someone had just called for me about solar panel,' so she already knows this is the solar callback; a full legitimacy intro may be less necessary on an inbound-initiated recontact.
coaching_implication: Even on recontact calls, a brief company/context anchor ('this is Carter with Ion, following up on the solar inquiry you had') costs nothing and protects against any doubt, especially since the customer had to correct a wrong assumption about the appointment's purpose.
